paragraphs.heading: A wall around a city
paragraphs.text: The Berlin Wall was a guarded concrete barrier that ringed West Berlin from 1961 to 1989, cutting it off from East Berlin and the rest of East Germany. It had an outer wall and an inner wall with guard towers, and a wide space between them, later called the death strip, that held anti-vehicle trenches, beds of nails and other defences. Along with the much longer border between East and West Germany, it became the physical symbol of the Iron Curtain that divided the Western and Eastern Blocs in the Cold War.

paragraphs.heading: A divided Germany
paragraphs.text: After World War II, what remained of Germany west of the Oder-Neisse line was split into four occupation zones, each run by one of the four Allied powers: the Soviet Union, the United States, the United Kingdom and France. Berlin, the capital, was also split into four sectors, even though the whole city lay inside the Soviet zone. Within two years, political divisions grew between the Soviets and the other three powers. In 1949 the Western zones became the Federal Republic of Germany, and on 7 October that year the German Democratic Republic, or East Germany, was declared.

paragraphs.heading: Blockade and airlift
paragraphs.text: In 1948, in response to Western moves to set up a separate federal government in their zones and to extend Marshall Plan aid to Germany, the Soviets started the Berlin Blockade. It stopped people, food and supplies from reaching West Berlin by land through the Soviet zone. The United States, the United Kingdom, France and several other countries answered with a huge airlift that supplied the city with food and other goods. In May 1949 Stalin lifted the blockade.

paragraphs.heading: Why the Wall went up
paragraphs.text: Living standards in West Berlin rose quickly, and people in the Soviet zone began leaving for the West to escape hunger, poverty and repression. This flight, called Republikflucht in Germany, cost the East workers it needed and, above all, highly educated people, a loss known as the brain drain. Before the Wall, 3.5 million East Germans, a fifth of the population, had left, many by crossing from East to West Berlin. Stopping this exodus was the main reason for building the Wall, which East Germany's government began on 13 August 1961.

paragraphs.heading: Two names for one wall
paragraphs.text: East Germany's government officially called it the Anti-Fascist Protection Rampart. Soviet Bloc propaganda claimed it protected people from fascists plotting to stop the building of a communist state. West Berlin's city government sometimes called it the Wall of Shame, a name coined by Mayor Willy Brandt because the Wall restricted freedom of movement.

paragraphs.heading: Escapes and deaths
paragraphs.text: After 1961, the deadly force behind the Wall stopped almost all emigration from the East. More than 100,000 people tried to escape, and over 5,000 got across. Estimates of those killed by East German authorities in and around Berlin range from 136 to more than 200.

paragraphs.heading: The Wall comes down
paragraphs.text: In 1989, revolutions in nearby Eastern Bloc countries, above all Poland and Hungary, and the Pan-European Picnic started a peaceful process in which the Iron Curtain largely broke. After the East German government announced on 9 November that its citizens could visit the West, crowds climbed onto the Wall and crossed it, joined by West Germans, while souvenir hunters chipped off pieces. Full demolition began on 13 June 1990 and ended in 1994. Germany was formally reunified on 3 October 1990.
